clue.text: Mutual cooperation needed to support withdrawal

blocks.note: to back someone is to support them
scratching is withdrawing a horse or competitor from an event

explanation.surface: Someone says mutual help is required to back a retreat or pull-out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Withdrawal' looks like the end of the sentence's meaning, but it is the sporting sense: a horse that is scratched is pulled from the race.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'you scratch my back and I'll scratch yours' gives a word for trading favours between allies.

clue.text: It's nonsense opposing the toreador's work

blocks.note: bull is slang for nonsense
fighting means opposing

explanation.surface: A complaint that it is ridiculous to oppose what a toreador does.
explanation.definitionFit: A toreador is a Spanish bullfighter, so his profession is the sport of the arena.

clue.text: Illnesses experienced in the Civil Service

indicators.note: something experienced in a body sits within it, so one piece goes inside the other

blocks.note: an old hand is an experienced one
CS is the abbreviation for Civil Service

explanation.surface: Sickness absences suffered by government staff.
explanation.walkthrough: The Civil Service is Britain's body of permanent government employees.
explanation.definitionFit: Common colds are minor viral infections, so they are a kind of illness.

clue.text: Unimportant moment on a railway

blocks.note: a second is a brief moment
taken as written
RY is the abbreviation for railway

explanation.surface: A trivial instant on a train line.
explanation.definitionFit: Something of secondary importance comes after the main thing, so it is minor.

clue.text: Like Auntie's story, made up and put about by cardinal

indicators.note: a made-up story is invented, so its letters are rearranged into something new
to be put about by something is to be surrounded by it, so one piece is wrapped in the other

blocks.note: cardinal red is a deep scarlet colour
a tale is a story

explanation.surface: An aunt's tale, invented and spread around by a churchman.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged story sits inside the colour after its first letter; 'cardinal' suggests a churchman but is the colour.
explanation.definitionFit: An aunt is a relative, so she is connected to you by family.

clue.text: Bob Cratchit's son gets mini on time nearly

indicators.note: nearly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: mini means very small
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Dickens character's boy acquires a small car, almost punctually.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dickens's A Christmas Carol, the clerk Bob Cratchit's sickly youngest child is this character.

clue.text: Boring half a hole with a buzz

indicators.note: only half of the word is wanted, so the back two letters are discarded

blocks.note: taken as written; only its first two letters are kept
a hum is a buzzing sound

explanation.surface: A dull hole in the ground that drones.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an exclamation of weariness, used as an adjective for something dull and routine.

clue.text: New dart is hard and somehow small in width

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for new
a dart is a small arrow
taken as written
H is the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard

explanation.surface: A fresh dart is tough and somewhat slender.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition paraphrases 'rather narrow': the -ish suffix means 'to some degree', which the first word of the definition loosely supplies.
explanation.definitionFit: The -ish ending means somewhat, so the word describes something fairly slim across.

clue.text: The shrub I call exotic

indicators.note: exotic means strange or foreign, so the letters appear in an unfamiliar order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone naming a plant they think foreign.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a garden bush with fragrant purple or white flower clusters.

clue.text: Heartless Lady North wants Cher's hangers

indicators.note: without a heart, the word loses its central letters and keeps only its ends

blocks.note: taken as written; its middle letters go
N is the abbreviation for North
the singer's name with the possessive s

explanation.surface: A cruel noblewoman covets the pop singer Cher's clothes hangers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hangers' suggests coat hangers, but it means people who hang others.
explanation.definitionFit: Lynch mobs execute people, usually by hanging, without any trial.

clue.text: If I talk of an egg, would you go away please?

definitions.text: If I talk of an egg

blocks.clueFragment: If I talk of an egg
blocks.note: first meaning: asking whether an egg can be whisked
second meaning: a polite request to leave, using the slang for go away

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is normally an expression of amazement; here it is read literally twice, once in the kitchen and once as an invitation to clear off.
explanation.definitionFit: Beat means whisk for an egg and is slang for leave, so the question fits both requests.

clue.text: Hunt to obtain some stocking material

blocks.note: to fish for something is to hunt for it
to net is to obtain

explanation.surface: Searching to get hold of hosiery fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an open mesh fabric used for tights and stockings.

clue.text: Lottery starting terrific boom, perhaps near LA

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept
perhaps signals the letters could be in some other possible order

blocks.note: the opening letter of terrific
taken as written
taken as written: Los Angeles

explanation.surface: A lottery sets off a huge economic boom near Los Angeles.
explanation.walkthrough: A tombola is a raffle where tickets are drawn from a revolving drum, common at British fêtes.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a game of chance with numbered tickets drawn for prizes, a kind of raffle.

clue.text: Italian city takes the cake

blocks.note: first meaning: the port in Liguria
second meaning: a rich fruit cake named after that port

explanation.surface: A city wins the prize, as in the idiom 'takes the cake'.
explanation.walkthrough: Genoa cake is a British fruit cake topped with almonds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ligurian seaport also names a rich almond-topped fruit cake.

clue.text: He sells the Guardian, which is fresh, wise and not without heart

indicators.note: removing the heart takes away the middle letter of the short word

blocks.note: fresh means new
a sage person is wise
taken as written; its middle letter goes

explanation.surface: Praise of the Guardian newspaper as fresh, wise and kind-hearted.
explanation.walkthrough: The setter's own paper is the example in the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A shopkeeper selling papers and magazines would stock the Guardian among others.

clue.text: Disguise my fist with dye and explain!

indicators.note: a disguise changes how something looks, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, with the link word left out

explanation.surface: An odd instruction to stain one's fist and then account for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the two parts of the fodder and is not part of it.
explanation.definitionFit: To clear away the mystery around something is to make it understandable.

clue.text: Ann is slow, surprising these relations

indicators.note: a surprising version is unexpected, so the letters come out in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Ann's slowness astonishes her family.
explanation.definitionFit: Daughters' husbands are relatives by marriage, which fits the plural relations.

clue.text: Sadly, Pa won't try this after-dinner drink

indicators.note: sadly suggests something gone wrong or badly arranged, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Regrettably, Father refuses to taste the digestif.
explanation.definitionFit: Port is a fortified wine traditionally passed round after a meal, and the tawny style is aged in wood.

clue.text: Long speech asks for love to share

blocks.note: love is zero in tennis, which looks like O
a ration is a share; 'to share' is to ration out

explanation.surface: A lengthy address pleads for affection to be spread around.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a formal public address, typically lengthy and delivered on a ceremonial occasion.

clue.text: Victory, yes, but I hurt PM in another way

indicators.note: doing something differently here means placing the same letters in a different order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A politician admits they won, but harmed the Prime Minister differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A triumph is a great success or a win over an opponent.

clue.text: Indian PM: he breaks vase on retiring

indicators.note: breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece goes into the other
retiring means withdrawing or going back, so the result is read backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
an urn is a kind of vase

explanation.surface: An Indian leader smashes a vase as he leaves office.
explanation.walkthrough: The pronoun goes inside the vessel and the whole lot is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: Jawaharlal Nehru was the first prime minister of independent India.

clue.text: Falls for a Monroe film

blocks.note: first meaning: the great waterfalls on the US–Canada border
second meaning: the 1953 thriller starring Marilyn Monroe

explanation.surface: Someone becomes infatuated with a Marilyn Monroe movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falls for' reads as a verb phrase about being smitten, but 'Falls' is a noun here.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the famous waterfalls and to the 1953 noir set beside them.

clue.text: Behave badly, putting tee in a cup!

indicators.note: putting one thing in another places it inside, so a piece goes into the vessel

blocks.note: taken as written
tee is the spoken name of the letter T

explanation.surface: Misbehaving by setting a golf tee inside a cup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' completes the container instruction: the letter goes inside 'a cup'.
explanation.definitionFit: To act up is to misbehave or play up, as a naughty child does.

clue.text: Mirror? I'm getting it put away

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
to put food away is to eat it

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether to store a looking glass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mirror' looks like a noun but is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To mirror someone is to copy their actions, reflecting them exactly.

clue.text: Counters where sailor just fails to get acid

indicators.note: falling just short of the whole word means its last letter is missed off

blocks.note: AB, able seaman, is a sailor
taken as written; its last letter is lost

explanation.surface: Shop counters where a seaman narrowly misses buying acid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Counters' suggests shop counters, but it means devices for counting.
explanation.definitionFit: An abacus is a bead frame used for counting, and this is its Latin plural.

clue.text: Mr Nicest shifted to holding moderate views

indicators.note: shifted means moved around, so the letters change position

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A very pleasant man moved to a middle-of-the-road position.
explanation.definitionFit: Centrism is the political stance between left and right, avoiding extremes.

clue.text: Inedible as toadstools? Look for the smallest!

indicators.note: looking for something means searching inside the clue words, where it lies concealed

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of the first word, the whole second word and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A foraging warning: toadstools are poisonous, so seek out the tiniest mushrooms.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark and exclamation make the clue read as advice to mushroom hunters; the answer is concealed across the first three words.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of little, it means of minimal size or amount.

clue.text: Points that wear out calling for a light reprimand

indicators.note: worn out means broken down, so the letters are knocked into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Tips that become blunt deserve a mild scolding.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a mild punishment or telling-off, far short of anything serious.
